rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the adjoining figure, AP and AQ are tangents to the circle with centre O. If reflex \(\angle POQ = 210^\circ\), the value of \(2x\) is
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - x is defined only in the drawing, as the angle PAQ between the two tangents at A; the drawing also marks the reflex angle 210 degrees at O. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
A radius is perpendicular to the tangent at its point of contact, so \(\angle OPA = \angle OQA = 90^\circ\).

The non-reflex angle \(\angle POQ = 360^\circ - 210^\circ = 150^\circ\). The angles of quadrilateral OPAQ add to \(360^\circ\):

\(x = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 150^\circ = 30^\circ\), so \(2x = 60^\circ\).

This is option (B) \(60^\circ\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem: The system of equations \(y + a = 0\) and \(2x = b\) has
rows.solution:
\(y + a = 0\) gives \(y = -a\), a horizontal line, and \(2x = b\) gives \(x = \dfrac{b}{2}\), a vertical line. They meet in exactly one point, whose x-coordinate is \(\dfrac{b}{2}\) and y-coordinate is \(-a\).

(The pair \(\left(-a, \dfrac{b}{2}\right)\) has the two coordinates the wrong way round.)

This is option (C) \(\left(\dfrac{b}{2}, -a\right)\) as its solution.

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: Which of the following equations does not have a real root ?
rows.solution:
\(x^2 + 1 = 0\) needs \(x^2 = -1\), and the square of a real number is never negative, so it has no real root.

The others: \(x^2 = 0\) has the root 0; \(2x - 1 = 3\) has the root 2; \(x^3 + x^2 = x^2(x + 1) = 0\) has the roots 0 and \(-1\).

This is option (C) \(x^2 + 1 = 0\).

rows.stem: The distance of point \(P(3a, 4a)\) from y-axis is
rows.solution:
The distance of a point from the y-axis is the absolute value of its x-coordinate: \(|3a|\). The options treat a as positive, and then the distance is \(3a\).

Strictly, the distance is \(|3a|\), so the answer \(3a\) holds only for \(a > 0\); for a negative a the distance would be \(-3a\).

This is option (A) \(3a\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** For two odd prime numbers \(x\) and \(y\), \((x \neq y)\), \(\text{LCM}(2x, 4y) = 4xy\)

**Reason (R) :** \(\text{LCM}(x, y)\) is a multiple of \(\text{HCF}(x, y)\).
rows.context:
Directions : In Question Numbers 19 and 20, a statement of Assertion (A) is followed by a statement of Reason (R).

Choose the correct option from the following :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
x and y are different odd primes, so \(2x = 2 \times x\) and \(4y = 2^2 \times y\). The LCM takes the highest power of each prime: \(\text{LCM}(2x, 4y) = 2^2 \times x \times y = 4xy\). The Assertion is true.

The LCM is a multiple of each number, and each number is a multiple of the HCF, so the LCM is a multiple of the HCF. The Reason is true.

The Assertion comes from the prime factorisation of \(2x\) and \(4y\), not from the Reason, so the Reason does not explain it.

Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
In the adjoining figure, AP = 1 cm, BP = 2 cm, AQ = 1.5 cm and AC = 4.5 cm.

Prove that \(\Delta APQ \sim \Delta ABC\). Hence find the length of PQ, if BC = 3.6 cm.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that P lies on AB and Q on AC, joined by PQ, is shown only in the drawing (labelled AP 1 cm, PB 2 cm, AQ 1.5 cm and AC 4.5 cm). Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
\(AB = AP + PB = 1 + 2 = 3\) cm.

In triangles APQ and ABC:

\(\dfrac{AP}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{AQ}{AC} = \dfrac{1.5}{4.5} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{AP}{AB} = \dfrac{AQ}{AC}\), and \(\angle PAQ = \angle BAC\) (common).

So \(\Delta APQ \sim \Delta ABC\) (SAS similarity). (The marking scheme prints the common angle as \(\angle ACP = \angle ACB\), a slip: the angle the two triangles share is the one at A.)

Corresponding sides are proportional: \(\dfrac{PQ}{BC} = \dfrac{AP}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(PQ = \dfrac{3.6}{3} = 1.2\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem:
A bag contains balls numbered 2 to 91 such that each ball bears a different number. A ball is drawn at random from the bag. Find the probability that

(i) it bears a 2– digit number

(ii) it bears a multiple of 1.
rows.solution:
The balls are numbered 2, 3, ..., 91, so there are \(91 - 2 + 1 = 90\) equally likely outcomes.

(i) The 2-digit numbers are 10 to 91: 82 numbers.

P(2-digit number) \(= \dfrac{82}{90} = \dfrac{41}{45}\).

(ii) Every whole number is a multiple of 1, so all 90 balls are favourable.

P(multiple of 1) \(= \dfrac{90}{90} = 1\). It is a sure event.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem:
Check whether the given system of equations is consistent or not. If consistent, solve graphically.

\(x - 2y = 0\)

\(2x + y = 0\)
rows.solution:
\(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-2}{1} = -2\). Since \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), the lines intersect, and the system is consistent with a unique solution.

Points on \(x - 2y = 0\):

| \(x\) | 0 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 0 | 1 | 2 |

Points on \(2x + y = 0\):

| \(x\) | \(-1\) | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | 2 | 0 | \(-2\) |

Plot both sets of points on the same axes and draw the two lines. Both pass through the origin, and they meet there.

The solution is \(x = 0\), \(y = 0\).

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: Find the zeroes of the polynomial \(r(x) = 4x^2 + 3x - 1\). Hence, write a polynomial whose zeroes are reciprocal of the zeroes of polynomial \(r(x)\).
rows.solution:
\(4x^2 + 3x - 1 = 4x^2 + 4x - x - 1 = 4x(x + 1) - 1(x + 1) = (4x - 1)(x + 1)\).

The zeroes of \(r(x)\) are \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) and \(-1\).

Their reciprocals are \(4\) and \(-1\).

Sum \(= 4 + (-1) = 3\); product \(= 4 \times (-1) = -4\).

The polynomial is \(x^2 - 3x - 4\) (any non-zero multiple of it).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem:
Fermentation tanks are designed in the form of cylinder mounted on a cone as shown below :

The total height of the tank is 3.3 m and height of conical part is 1.2 m. The diameter of the cylindrical as well as conical part is 1 m. Find the capacity of the tank. If the level of liquid in the tank is 0.7 m from the top, find the surface area of the tank in contact with liquid.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - an unlabelled drawing of the tank, a cylinder standing on an inverted cone; the stem states the shape and every dimension. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Radius \(r = 0.5\) m, height of the cone \(h = 1.2\) m, and height of the cylinder \(H = 3.3 - 1.2 = 2.1\) m. Take \(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\).

Capacity of the tank \(=\) volume of cylinder \(+\) volume of cone

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.5^2 \times 2.1 + \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.5^2 \times 1.2 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.25 \times (2.1 + 0.4) = \dfrac{55}{28} \approx 1.96\) m\(^3\).

The liquid is 0.7 m below the top, so it fills the whole cone and \(2.1 - 0.7 = 1.4\) m of the cylinder.

Slant height of the cone: \(l = \sqrt{1.2^2 + 0.5^2} = \sqrt{1.69} = 1.3\) m.

Surface in contact with the liquid \(=\) curved surface of the 1.4 m of cylinder \(+\) curved surface of the cone

\(= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.5 \times 1.4 + \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.5 \times 1.3 = 4.4 + 2.04 = 6.44\) m\(^2\) (approximately).
